"We'll all be jobless as developers in 2 years." 🤖

One view at my table at the Claude Code meetup at Mesh Oslo last Wednesday. We spent most of the evening on it.

🧭 My bet is the opposite. The work moves up a level: what to build, why, and how. The agent writes the code, but a human still oversees it and owns whether what ships is right.

🛡️ Martin A Kraft pitched a safety and ethics focused Claude meetup, and the whole table backed it: Dario Fernandez Castellon, Kai Norman, Yufei Wang and Rune Horneland. Mesh Oslo GritAI Aleksander Stensby, count us in.

If your team already ships mostly agent-written code: where did the human work go? 👇

#ClaudeCode #SoftwareEngineering #ResponsibleAI #OsloTech

Yesterday I posted that my AI coding bill dropped 3× because of context size, not the newer model. Then I did the full analysis. Context size was right. "Not the model" was wrong.

38 days of my own Claude Code logs, priced at list rates: about $4,725. That's an estimate from my transcripts, not an invoice.

Where it went: 6% paid for the model writing answers. 94% paid for re-sending conversation history it had already seen. At 800k tokens of history, one message cost about 20× what it costs under 50k, for the same answer.

The part I didn't expect: the cache expires after 5 minutes. Get a coffee, check Slack, come back, and the whole history is written again at a premium. 81% of that re-writing cost came after gaps of 5 minutes or more, and the biggest bucket was 5 to 15 minutes. Not task switches. Coffee. ☕

At the Claude Community meetup at Mesh Oslo this week, Aleksander Stensby talked about /clear and /compact. I've used Claude Code daily since May and that was the first time I'd heard of either.

📉 So I simulated the same 38 days as if I'd used them.

- /clear when coming back after an hour: −49%
- /compact once history passes 150k tokens: −56%
- Both: −59%

Now the correction. I ran /compact by hand exactly zero times in 38 days, so something else kept the context small. On the old model, Claude Code auto-compacted at ~1M tokens, which I hit about once a week. On the newer model it compacts at ~167k. The model switch is what shrank the context.

So the model did matter, just not the way I thought. It didn't think cheaper. It forgot sooner.

If you live in Claude Code or a similar tool every day: do you clear and compact by hand, or let the tool decide? And has anyone found a threshold where cost drops but answer quality holds? 👇

#ClaudeCode #DeveloperProductivity

Most meetups have a stage and an audience. Last night's Claude Community Conversation at Mesh Oslo had neither 🪑 About 50 of us, split into tables, and two questions to work through: 👉 What does AI mean for my job? 👉 What is AI doing to me, my kids, my community? Five prompts per question, ending on "where do we start?". It sounds tidy on paper. In practice, our table spent two hours on where the world is heading, what happens to the work we do, and what kind of future our kids are walking into.

🤝 What made it work was the mix. Enthusiasts and skeptics at the same table, some worried about AI going badly wrong, others worried about being left behind, and nobody had to shrink their view to fit the room.

🔐 The topic we kept coming back to was the OpenAI / Hugging Face incident. My take: the AI didn't do anything a good team of hackers couldn't. Same problem, same setup, and I'd bet they land in the same place. It would just take them months instead of weeks. The capability isn't new. The speed is, and that's the part worth worrying about.

🙏 Thanks to Aleksander Stensby for organising and to Anthropic for sponsoring. And to Dario Fernandez Castellon, Martin A Kraft, Rune Horneland, Kai Norman and Yufei Wang: thanks for the honesty, the openness, and for sitting through two hours of my rants 😄

🚀 Next up is the Impact Lab in October, where we try to build answers to some of the questions we raised. Count me in (If my boss at home and boss at work permits 😅)

📸 Photo credits: Simon Sebergsen. I was too busy talking to take any myself. Eagerly waiting for the official ones to be shared from the event.

I told my team that switching to a newer AI model cut my token bill 🤖💸 Then I actually measured it 😅

📊 Two weeks of my own logs said: yes, usage dropped 3×. But the new model wasn't the reason.

🧠 The real reason was memory. I'd been running with a huge context window, so the AI re-read a giant conversation on every single message. When I stopped doing that, the bill shrank 📉 Same kind of work, a third of the tokens.

✨ The new model helped too, just a lot less than I thought.

💡 Lesson for me: what you feed the AI costs more than which AI you pick. Start fresh often, and keep the conversation lean 🧹 Anyone else measured theirs, or are we all running on vibes? 👇

♻️ 672,007 tonnes of CO2e avoided in a year, just from people buying and selling used stuff across Vend 's marketplaces. FINN.no – mulighetenes marked Blocket Tori.fi dba.dk

That's from our 2025 Second Hand Effect Report, released today (PDF attached, longer report link in comments). It's an estimate, not a measurement, and the report says so upfront. I like that. The direction is what matters: second-hand should be the first choice, not the fallback.

At home it already is. Most of what we buy comes from FINN, Fretex or the local bruktbutikk. And anything we no longer use that still has life left goes back on FINN. Quite often it's given away for free, but it doesn't go in the bin.

The number that surprised me more: 61% of sellers use what they earn to cover everyday household expenses. Selling your old pram isn't only about the climate, for many people it's what keeps the monthly budget working.

I get to build the messaging that buyers and sellers use to strike these deals. Nice to see what all those conversations add up to. 💬

What was the last thing you bought second-hand, or gave away instead of throwing out?

When the CEO of the world's largest sovereign wealth fund recommends a Bollywood revenge saga, a fellow Oslo resident from India has to chime in. 🎬 Nicolai Tangen is right - #Dhurandhar is a spectacle. #RanveerSingh is magnetic, #AdityaDhar holds tension like few in Hindi cinema right now, and across 3.5+ hours it mostly earns its runtime. Special mention for #GauravGera, hats off dude.

The "A" certificate is honest, though. Violence isn't just present — it's the film's default setting, dialled so far past impact it tips into numbness. Visceral becomes gratuitous more than once.

Where it separates itself is sound. 🎧 Instead of chasing new chartbusters, they reached for songs already etched in collective memory — "Aari Aari," "Tamma Tamma Loge" — and placed them with real care to trigger instant recognition and lift the emotion. A familiar hook lands feeling a new one still has to earn. In a film built on excess, that instinct is what stayed with me.

Bloody, loud, a touch too long — and still worth the ticket. Number 2 = 1, as Nicolai put it. Agreement across Norway and India on this one.

💬 If you've seen it — did the old-song callbacks land for you, or did the sheer violence drown them out?

🔄 14 months ago, I posted about retiring my sticker collection for a fresh laptop. Clean slate. Fresh start. All of it.

The laptop is fully covered again. A few earned their place — "have fun & get sh**t done" (our department motto), a winter-edition conference tee that beats anything on the market.

Lesson from 2025, one year in: peeling stickers off was the ritual, not the point. Laptops get covered again because that's what happens when you actually use them.

👇 If you peeled yours off tomorrow — which sticker do you replace first?

🤖 A year ago I published Taming the Machine — arguing AI regulation should borrow Wall Street's playbook 💰 and GDPR's individual safeguards 🔒. Reading it back today, some of it holds up. Some of it clearly doesn't.

✅ What still stands: circuit breakers on high-stakes AI systems, silos to limit blast radius when things fail, mandatory explainability audits, purpose limitation on training data. Regulating for risk containment, not trying to forecast where AI is going. The industry has drifted further toward the failure modes those are designed to contain, not less.

❌ What doesn't: I spent too much of the piece on institutional form — "AI SEC", "AI SEBI" — as if the shape of the regulator was the interesting question. It isn't. Compute governance is the lever that actually moves.

⚡ Two tools that showed up during the last stretch of learning genAI + living inside Claude Code. Both earned their place. For very different reasons.

🎭 Playwright — deterministic, boring, does exactly what you tell it. Not AI. But paired with Claude Code the loop gets unreasonable: agent writes code, Playwright drives the browser, agent watches the trace, fixes, re-runs. No human in the middle. Bonus: per-test video recordings turn "make a demo clip" from an afternoon into a command.

🕷 BrowserMCP — the AI-adjacent one, and where the Skeptic hat goes on. Handing an LLM a live handle on my real browser session — cookies, tabs, everything I'm logged into — is a bad default. Wide privilege surface for a thing whose failure mode is confident wrongness. Nothing I'd point at production. But for scoped, local, "look at this page and click that" work on a throwaway sandbox, it removes the last bit of glue that still needed a human.

The rule I'm settling on: Playwright when I need certainty. BrowserMCP when I need speed on work I don't mind blowing up. Not competing — different jobs.

My AI Skeptic & Enthusiast reflex hesitates before installing third-party tools — each install is another dependency, another attack surface, another thing to keep updated — so I took the shapes people suggested and built local versions instead of adopting the tools.

🎨 Terminal background per codebase. `tbg <path>` writes an OSC 11 escape to iTerm2, and a hard-coded mapping means the moment I switch codebases the terminal changes colour. Peripheral awareness, zero cognitive load. Rendering the colours is a one-liner — deciding the mapping took longer than writing the script.

🔗 Per-project memory that auto-loads. Every project gets a MEMORY.md that Claude reads at session start. Small typed memory files sit alongside it — user preferences, project state, references — with [[wiki-style]] links between them. Cross-session context is now a filesystem, not a stitched-together conversation history.

🧠 Session sprawl is still only half-solved.

Nordic-marketplace data at real scale, product surfaces that actually ship, and a team that argues about the right things.

If you want AI work where the output lands in front of users next week - not in a slide deck - this one's worth a look.

⚡ Most developers, architects and tech folks I know are now running some flavour of CLI AI orchestrator - Claude Code, OpenCode, Copilot CLI.

I started using Claude Code in May after returning from paternity leave, and went all-in after summer. Three things are actively slowing me down:

     🧠 Session sprawl. Multiple terminals, multiple sessions, multiple tasks in flight. Keeping track of what's running where takes real cognitive load.

     🔗 No shared memory across sessions. When two parallel sessions produce related output, stitching them together is manual work.

    🎨 No visual cue for what I'm working in. Production code, a personal prototype, a hackathon repo — they all look the same in the terminal. Easy to type the wrong thing in the wrong window.

👇 If you're further along the Claude Code path than I am, how are you solving these? Less interested in tool names, more in the workflow shape that actually holds up for you.

Trying to come up with my own solutions but haven't landed on anything concrete yet  -curious to see how much of it overlaps with what the crowd here is already doing.

🧠💥 AI won’t wait—and neither should we.

When one software glitch can ground planes and shut down hospitals across 100+ countries (like the recent CrowdStrike outage), imagine what an unchecked black-box AI could do.

We’re standing at a crossroads:
➡️ One path leads to innovation with accountability.
➡️ The other? Silent collapse, invisible causes, no one to blame.

“Taming the Machine: What AI Regulation Can Learn from Wall Street and GDPR” - In this piece, I explore how we can stop guessing what AI might do—and start building guardrails that actually work.

🔍 Key takeaways:
✅ Agnostic regulation—like the SEC handles markets
✅ Explainability audits—like GDPR ensures individual rights
✅ Circuit breakers, kill switches, bias testing
✅ Why siloed systems matter—and global cooperation matters more

👉 If AI is already making decisions that shape justice, medicine, and markets, don’t we owe it the same scrutiny we give stock trades?

Let’s build resilience, not just regulation. Feedback and discussion welcome 👇
